newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Hani killer fondly recalls role in white S.Africa.
newsitem.headline: Hani killer fondly recalls role in white S.Africa.

text.p: A right-winger seeking amnesty for murdering South African Communist Party leader Chris Hani, fondly told the truth commission on Tuesday of his proud achievements in upholding a bygone apartheid age.

Clive Derby-Lewis, a one-time member of parliament for the right-wing Conservative Party, was testifying in public for the first time about the 1993 murder of a popular hero that also nearly killed off the fragile transition to democracy.
He and Polish immigrant Janusz Walus have applied to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission for amnesty, which they may get if they tell the full truth and if their act was found to be political.

"The Almighty Father provided me with certain talents and I consider it my responsibility to use these where and when I can," Derby-Lewis, 61, told the amnesty committee hearing in Pretoria's imposing City Hall.
"Ever since I can remember I have had a driving ambition... to be involved in the future of my country," he said as he began to outline the motives that led to the murder.
Dressed in a dark blazer, the stocky, moustachioed man smiled to himself and chuckled as he recalled his record as a proud white citizen of the old apartheid state.
He happily did his military service, became mayor of a town near Johannesburg and told how he tried his best to stop private schools there admitting blacks and lowering standards.
Derby-Lewis moved to the right as the ruling National Party considered compromise with the black majority.

He helped found the Conservative Party and jointly plotted murder with Walus, who gunned Hani down outside his home on Easter Saturday 1993, threatening the worst crisis in the long negotiations that led to free elections a year later.
Both men were sentenced to death.
The sentence still stands and they sit on death row in Pretoria Central Prison, even though a constitutional ban on state executions means they are effectively serving life.
Derby-Lewis's wife Gaye was a co-defendant but was acquitted in a trial that also found no proof of a wider conspiracy.
Hani's family, the Communist Party and President Nelson Mandela's ruling African National Congress are fiercely opposing amnesty.
Their lawyer, George Bizos -- who defended Mandela in the 1964 trial where he was sent to jail for life -- says he will try to prove the applicants have not told the full truth.
He wants to produce statements the three made after their arrest and which could shed new light on Gaye Derby-Lewis's role. The amnesty committee still has to decide if he can do so.

Walus, 44, is due to testify after Derby-Lewis. A virulent anti-communist, he came to South Africa in 1981 to escape martial-rule Poland, saying he believed the Afrikaners would never let their land succumb to such a godless ideology.
The hearing, attended by communists, leading ANC figures and white right-wingers, is due to last for two weeks but the committee's decision might take much longer.

Derby-Lewis painted a picture of a man still committed to the ideal of separate homelands for South Africa's many races, rather than the multiracial society whose advent he had tried to fight by plotting Hani's murder.
"My loyalty to South Africa, its people and the party has never been in question," he solemnly stated.
